title: What quality means on a project
blurb: Define quality as fitness for purpose or conformance, for outputs and processes, and spot gold plating.
question: A council's new library app does everything in its agreed specification and residents find it easy to use. A councillor calls it 'low quality' because a neighbouring council's app has a flashier design and extra features. Using the APM definition, how should the app's quality be judged?

teach.body: In project management, quality is the fitness for purpose, or the degree of conformance, of the outputs of a process or of the process itself. In plain English: does it do the job it was meant to do, and does it match what was agreed? Quality is NOT about being the most expensive, the most advanced or the most luxurious. A simple output that meets its requirements is a quality output.

teach.h: Two lenses on the same idea

rows.label: The question
values: Does it do the job needed?
Does it match what was agreed?

teach.caption: Both lenses point the same way: quality is judged against the agreed requirements and the purpose, not against luxury.

teach.body: The definition covers two things. The outputs of a process: the products or deliverables, such as a building, an app or a training course. And the process itself: the way the work is done, such as the design method, the build procedure or the testing approach. A sound, consistently followed process makes good outputs far more likely, so a project manager cares about the quality of both.

teach.caption: Exam wording often says 'the outputs of a process or the process itself'. Both halves count.

teach.body: Riverside Council's library app must let residents search the catalogue, reserve books and renew loans, and must meet accessibility standards. The finished app does all of this reliably. A councillor compares it with a neighbouring app that has animated graphics and a chat feature, and calls Riverside's 'low quality'. He is wrong: Riverside's app conforms to its requirements and is fit for purpose, so it IS a quality output. The rival may be a higher grade, but grade is not quality.

teach.h: Quality is not the same as grade
teach.caption: Grade describes the category or level of features. A low-grade output can be high quality; a high-grade output can be poor quality.

teach.text: Gold plating is NOT quality. Adding extras nobody asked for (premium materials, bonus features, a higher specification) uses time, money and effort the project did not plan for, and adds risk. The exam's favourite distractors describe quality as 'the best available', 'exceeding requirements' or 'the most features'. All three are wrong.

items: Quality: the fitness for purpose, or the degree of conformance, of the outputs of a process or of the process itself.
It applies to products (outputs) AND to processes.
It is judged against the agreed requirements, not against luxury, price or rival products.
Gold plating (unrequested extras) is not quality; it wastes resources and adds risk.
Grade is the level of features. Low grade can still be high quality.

summary: You can now define quality as the fitness for purpose, or degree of conformance, of outputs and of processes, and judge it against the agreed requirements. You can also explain why gold plating and a higher grade are not the same as quality.

A.q: Complete the statement: quality is the fitness for purpose, or the degree of ______, of the outputs of a process or of the process itself.
A.why: Quality is the fitness for purpose, or the degree of conformance, of the outputs of a process or of the process itself.

whyNot.1: Innovation is about novelty. An output can be innovative and still fail its requirements.
whyNot.2: Efficiency is about the resources used, not whether the output meets its requirements.
whyNot.3: Affordability is a cost measure. Spending less or more does not make an output conform.

A.q: To which of the following does the term 'quality' apply on a project?
A.why: The definition covers the outputs of a process and the process itself, so quality applies to both.

whyNot.0: The definition explicitly includes 'the process itself', so processes count too.
whyNot.1: The definition starts with the outputs of a process, so outputs count too.
whyNot.3: Budget and schedule are constraints alongside quality, not what quality describes.

A.q: An office fit-out specifies hard-wearing vinyl flooring. The designer installs marble instead, at extra cost, because it looks better. What is this an example of?
A.why: Gold plating means adding features or a higher specification that nobody asked for. It uses unplanned time and money and is not quality.

whyNot.0: Quality control is inspecting and testing outputs against criteria, not upgrading them.
whyNot.2: Vinyl was already fit for purpose. Marble goes beyond the need rather than meeting it.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance checks that processes are followed; it does not upgrade materials.

B.q: Which statement best describes an output that is 'fit for purpose'?
options: It does the job its users need it to do
It is the most advanced option available
It was delivered under its agreed budget
It has more features than were requested
B.why: Fit for purpose means the output does the job it was intended to do for its users.

whyNot.1: Being the most advanced is about grade, not whether it meets the need.
whyNot.2: Coming in under budget is a cost result, not a quality judgement.
whyNot.3: Extra features beyond the request are gold plating, not fitness for purpose.

B.q: A charity's new donor database meets every requirement in its specification. A trustee complains that a rival charity's system looks slicker. How should the database's quality be judged?
options: Poor, because a rival product looks better
Good, as it meets its agreed requirements
Unknown until it is compared with rivals
Poor, as it lacks premium design features
B.why: Quality is judged against the agreed requirements. The database meets them all, so it is a quality output.

whyNot.0: Rival products are not the yardstick; the agreed requirements are.
whyNot.2: No comparison is needed. Quality is judged against this project's requirements.
whyNot.3: Premium design is a matter of grade. Lacking it does not make the output poor quality.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are part of the definition of quality?
1. Conformance to requirements
2. The highest available grade
3. Fitness for purpose
4. Delivery ahead of schedule
B.why: Quality is fitness for purpose or the degree of conformance. Grade and early delivery are not part of the definition.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the highest grade is not quality, and can be gold plating.
whyNot.2: Neither the highest grade nor early delivery is part of the definition.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: early delivery is about time, not quality.

C.q: A team's testing procedure is followed exactly on every release and is shown to catch faults reliably. Which aspect of quality does this mainly demonstrate?
C.why: Quality applies to the process itself as well as its outputs. A reliable, consistently followed testing procedure shows process quality.

whyNot.1: Grade describes the level of a product's features, not how well a procedure works.
whyNot.2: Gold plating is adding unrequested extras to outputs, which is not happening here.
whyNot.3: Scope is what the project will deliver, not how well its procedures work.

C.q: Why is gold plating considered a problem on a project?
options: It reduces the grade of the final product
It is only permitted in iterative projects
It always makes outputs fail acceptance
It spends resources on unrequested extras
C.why: Gold plating adds features or specification nobody asked for, using time, money and effort the project did not plan for, and adding risk.

whyNot.0: Gold plating raises the grade rather than reducing it; the problem is the wasted resources.
whyNot.1: Gold plating is undesirable in any life cycle, not permitted in one type.
whyNot.2: A gold-plated output may still pass acceptance; the problem is unplanned cost and risk.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the meaning of quality on a project?
options: It is judged against agreed requirements
A low-cost output can be of good quality
A higher specification is always better
It applies to processes as well as outputs
C.why: A higher specification is not automatically better quality. Going beyond the requirements can be gold plating.

whyNot.0: This is consistent: requirements are the yardstick for quality.
whyNot.1: This is consistent: a cheap output that meets its requirements is a quality output.
whyNot.3: This is consistent: the definition covers the process itself as well as its outputs.

reteach.title: Think of ordering a birthday cake
reteach.question: You order a nut-free chocolate cake for 20 guests. Two bakers deliver very different cakes. Which one is the quality cake?

blocks.body: Baker A delivers a plain chocolate cake that serves 20 and contains no nuts. Baker B delivers a stunning five-tier cake decorated with almonds. Baker B's cake is higher grade and cost far more, but it contains nuts, so it fails the requirement and is not fit for purpose. Baker A's cake is the quality cake: it conforms to the order and does the job. Baker B also gold plated: four extra tiers nobody asked for.

blocks.text: Impressive is not the same as quality. If it misses the agreed requirements, it is poor quality, however good it looks.

explain.body: An output is fit for purpose when it does the job it was created to do for the people who will use it. A wheelchair ramp is fit for purpose if wheelchair users can get in safely and easily.

explain.h: From need to fit for purpose

test.q: A new ticket machine sells tickets quickly and reliably, exactly as passengers need. Which part of the quality definition does this mainly show?
test.why: The machine does the job its users need, which is fitness for purpose.

whyNot.0: Gold plating means unrequested extras; nothing extra is described.
whyNot.1: Grade is the level of features. Nothing here suggests a premium specification.
whyNot.3: An audit examines processes; this describes how well the output does its job.

explain.body: Conformance asks how closely an output matches its agreed requirements and specification. If the specification says the ramp gradient is 1 in 15 and it is built to 1 in 15, it conforms.

test.q: A bridge's steelwork is measured and matches every dimension in its specification. Which term best describes this?
test.why: Matching the agreed specification is conformance, one half of the quality definition.

whyNot.0: Gold plating goes beyond the specification; this matches it exactly.
whyNot.1: Grade is about the level of features, not matching a specification.
whyNot.2: Value for money compares cost with benefit; it is not part of the quality definition.

explain.body: Quality covers both the outputs (the products and deliverables) and the processes that create and check them. A good process, consistently followed, makes good outputs more likely.

test.q: Which statement about the scope of the term 'quality' is correct?
options: It covers outputs but never processes
It covers processes but never outputs
It covers only the final handover
It covers both outputs and processes
test.why: Quality is the fitness for purpose or conformance of the outputs of a process or of the process itself: both are covered.

whyNot.0: The definition includes 'the process itself', so processes are covered.
whyNot.1: The definition includes 'the outputs of a process', so outputs are covered.
whyNot.2: Quality matters throughout the project, not only at handover.

explain.body: Grade is the level or category of features (basic or premium). Quality is meeting the requirements. Adding unrequested extras is gold plating: it costs time and money and adds risk without adding quality.

test.q: How does 'quality' differ from 'grade' on a project?
options: They are two words for the same idea
Grade measures conformance to the spec
test.why: Quality is about meeting the requirements and being fit for purpose. Grade is the level or category of features.

whyNot.0: Costlier materials raise the grade or cost; they do not define quality.
whyNot.2: They are different: a low-grade output can be high quality.
whyNot.3: Conformance is part of quality, not of grade.
